article.title: Before You Buy A Standing Desk: The Honest Version
article.meta_description: Standing desks fail in three predictable ways: wobble, a dead controller, and a height that never quite suits you. Here is how to avoid all three.
intro: The health argument for standing desks is thinner than the marketing suggests, and pretending otherwise sets you up for disappointment. What is solid is narrower and more useful: being able to change position during a long workday reduces the specific aches that come from not moving.

Buy one for that reason and it is a good purchase. Buy one expecting it to fix a sedentary life and it becomes an expensive coat stand within three months, which is what happens to a surprising number of them.

sections.heading: Stability is the whole product
paragraphs: Every standing desk wobbles at full extension - that is basic physics with a tall column and a load on top. The question is how much, and at what height. A desk that shakes when you type at standing height is one you will stop raising, which means you paid for an adjustment feature you do not use.

Weight is the cheapest available proxy for stability here. Heavier frames with a wide footprint and a two- or three-stage column wobble less than light single-stage ones. Cross-braces and a solid desktop-to-frame connection matter more than any motor specification. If the listing does not state the desk's own weight, that omission is itself informative.
bullets: Two-stage or three-stage columns reach lower and higher than single-stage ones, and are generally stiffer.
Dual motors lift more evenly and handle heavier loads; single-motor desks are fine for light setups.
Frame weight and footprint do more for wobble than motor power does.

sections.heading: Get the height range right before anything else
paragraphs: This is the most common regret, and it is entirely avoidable. The range you need depends on your own proportions, not on an average. Check the desk's minimum height against your seated elbow height - if the desk cannot go low enough, you will be typing with your shoulders lifted all day, which is worse than the problem you started with.

Equally, check the maximum against your standing elbow height. People over roughly six feet find many budget desks top out a few centimetres too low, and then spend the money anyway and live with a monitor that sits below eye level.
Measure yourself first: seated elbow height with your feet flat, and standing elbow height with shoulders relaxed. Then compare those two numbers to the specification, not to the marketing photo.

sections.heading: The controller fails before the motor does
paragraphs: When an electric desk stops working, it is usually the control box or the handset rather than the motors. That makes the warranty terms and spare-part availability more important than the motor brand on the specification sheet.

Look for two things: a warranty that covers the electronics for as long as the frame, and a manufacturer that sells replacement controllers. A desk with a lifetime frame warranty and a one-year electronics warranty is telling you which part they expect to fail.

sections.heading: Assembly, and the desktop question
paragraphs: Most of these arrive flat and are heavy. A two-person job for the larger sizes, and the desktop is the awkward part - lifting a full-size board and flipping it onto the frame alone is how people damage both. Check the delivered weight and plan accordingly before it arrives on a day you are alone.

Separately, decide whether you want the manufacturer's desktop or your own. Buying the frame alone and fitting a board you chose is often cheaper and gives a better surface, but you must match the mounting points and make sure the board is not so heavy or so flexible that it sags between the frame rails.

sections.heading: What you actually use daily
paragraphs: Memory presets turn out to be the feature that decides whether the desk gets used. Without them, adjusting means holding a button and watching, so you do it twice and then stop. With two or three saved heights, switching takes a second and you do it several times a day without deciding to.

Everything else is secondary. Cable management trays are useful and cheap to add later. Anti-collision sensors are worth having if children or pets are around, because the desk will otherwise keep driving into whatever it meets. A built-in USB hub sounds convenient and is usually slower and less accessible than one on your monitor.

sections.heading: Who should not buy one
paragraphs: If your current problem is a bad chair, fix the chair first - a desk that lets you stand badly is not an improvement. If you work in short bursts away from home, a laptop stand and a kitchen counter deliver most of the benefit for a fraction of the cost and none of the floor space.

And if the honest answer is that you would rather not stand while working, do not buy one on the strength of an article. A good task chair and a habit of walking every hour gets you most of the same outcome.

faq.q: How do I know what height range I need?
faq.a: Measure twice. Sitting: feet flat on the floor, shoulders relaxed, elbows bent at roughly ninety degrees - measure from floor to elbow. Standing: same shoulder position, measure floor to elbow again. The desk must cover both numbers with a little margin. Most regrets in this category come from buying before measuring.

faq.q: Are dual motors worth it over a single motor?
faq.a: For a full-size desktop with a monitor arm and a heavy setup, yes - two motors lift more evenly, handle more load, and put less strain on each drive. For a small desk with a laptop and one monitor, a single motor is adequate and cheaper. The difference shows up over years rather than weeks.

faq.q: Why do standing desks wobble, and can it be fixed?
faq.a: A tall column carrying a load above its base will deflect; the question is how much. Wobble reduces with frame mass, a wider footprint, more column stages, and a rigid desktop-to-frame connection. Tightening every fastener after the first fortnight helps, because they settle. It cannot be engineered out completely at full extension.

The control box or handset, in most reported cases, rather than the motors. That is why the electronics warranty and the availability of a replacement controller matter more than the motor specification. A desk marketed with a lifetime frame warranty and one year on the electronics is being honest about which part they expect to replace.

faq.q: Is standing all day actually better?
faq.a: No, and no serious recommendation says so. Prolonged static standing brings its own problems - legs, feet, lower back. The benefit comes from changing position several times a day rather than from either posture being correct. Treat the desk as a way to move more, not a way to stand more.

conclusion: Measure your two elbow heights, then look for a frame that covers both with margin, weighs enough to stay still, and carries a warranty on its electronics that matches the warranty on its steel. Those four checks will out-perform any amount of brand comparison.
Then buy the memory-preset handset. It is the difference between a desk you adjust six times a day and one you adjust twice in the first week.
